title: Designing PSS and SVC Parameters simultaneously through the Improved Quantum Algorithm in the Multi-machine Power System
journal_or_venue: Journal of Intelligent Procedures in Electrical Technology
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a coordinated design of Power System Stabilizers (PSS) and Static VAR Compensator (SVC) parameters using an improved quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm (QEA). The method is validated on Kundur's four-machine and the New England 39-bus test systems, showing improved damping of electromechanical oscillations, reduced settling times and better ITAE performance compared with PSO and BFO approaches.
methodology_description: The study formulates coordinated tuning of Power System Stabilizers (PSS) and a Static VAR Compensator (SVC) as a dynamic optimization problem for multi-machine power systems. Dynamic models used include a fifth-order synchronous machine model for each generator, a classical lead-lag PSS with washout filter, and an SVC represented with a PI controller for reactive current control. The objective is to minimize an Integral of Time-weighted Absolute Error (ITAE) of rotor speed deviations summed over machines. Controller parameter bounds are enforced (e.g. PI: 0.1 < Kpt < 5, 100 < Kit < 500; T2,T4 in (0.1,10); other ranges from cited refs). Optimization is performed using a Quantum-inspired Evolutionary Algorithm (QEA): solutions are encoded as qubit vectors (equal initial amplitudes), binary candidates are generated by observation, evaluated using the ITAE objective via time-domain simulation, and qubits are updated with quantum rotation gates (qugate) according to a rotation-angle rule (Table 1). The QEA results are compared against PSO and BFO-based coordinated tuning. Time-domain simulations (fault/transient scenarios) are run on two benchmark power systems (Kundur two-area 4-machine and New England 39-bus) using the PSAT toolbox; performance metrics reported include ITAE, settling times, terminal voltages, and optimized controller parameter sets.
experimental_setup: Time-domain simulation using the PSAT toolbox. Test systems: Kundur two-area four-machine system (with VAR compensator at midline) and New England 39-bus system. Fault scenarios: symmetric three-phase faults (100 ms and 200 ms) at specified buses (e.g., bus 8 in Kundur, bus 4 in New England); additional steady-state tests such as ±5% terminal voltage changes. Models: 5th-order generator dynamics, lead-lag PSS with washout, SVC modeled with PI controller (added Kr and Tr in NE39 case). Some simplifying assumptions applied (e.g., T2=T4=0.1, T1=T3 in NE39).
experiment_input: Benchmark power system models (Kundur 2-area 4-machine and New England 39-bus) from literature. Inputs include machine parameters (fifth-order models), network topology and line data from standard test cases, initial operating points from references, and disturbance profiles: 3-phase faults at specified buses with durations 100 ms (and 200 ms for Kundur). Controller parameter search spaces: Kpss and T1..T4 (PSS), Kpt and Kit (SVC PI); parameter bounds reported in paper (e.g., 0.1<Kpt<5, 100<Kit<500, 0.1<T2,T4<10). No external data preprocessing beyond model setup is described.
experiment_process: 1) Encode PSS and SVC parameters into QEA qubit representation (initially equal probability amplitudes). 2) Observe qubit vectors to generate a binary population of candidate parameter sets. 3) Decode binary candidates into real-valued controller parameters within specified bounds. 4) For each candidate, run time-domain simulation (PSAT) for the chosen fault/profile and compute ITAE = sum_i ∫ t * |Δω_i(t)| dt. 5) Identify best-so-far solution. 6) Update qubits using a rotation gate (qugate) with rotation angles chosen according to a sign table (Table 1) based on comparison between candidate and best solution. 7) Repeat observation, evaluation, and qubit update until termination criterion (not explicitly specified) is met. 8) Report optimized controller parameters and performance metrics; compare to baseline PSO and BFO tuned controllers by running same simulations. The pipeline uses QEA hyper-operators as described by Han & Kim (rotation gate, observation), but the paper does not specify population size, number of generations, or random seeds.

reproducibility_notes: The paper reports the models used (5th-order machine, PSS structure, SVC PI) and test cases (Kundur 4-machine, New England 39-bus) and states simulation via the PSAT toolbox, but does not provide code or scripts. Some algorithmic hyperparameters are not reported (population size, number of generations/iterations, termination criterion, random seeds), which limits exact reproducibility. Parameter bounds and many optimized result values are reported in tables, enabling partial replication if using the same test cases and PSAT. No public repository or code availability statement is provided.
key_findings: [supported] A quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm (QEA) was applied to simultaneously tune Power System Stabilizer (PSS) and Static VAR Compensator (SVC) parameters in multi-machine power system models (Kundur 4-machine and New England 39-bus).

[supported] In time-domain fault simulations QEA produced faster damping and shorter settling times for generator speed deviations compared with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Bacteria Foraging Optimization (BFO) in the tested scenarios.
[supported] The Integral of Time-weighted Absolute Error (ITAE) objective was lower for QEA (0.0138) than for PSO (0.0251) and BFO (0.0162) in the 4-machine test case reported.

[supported] Specific numerical improvements reported include reduced settling times for generators in the Kundur 4-machine tests (e.g., G1: 6.1128 s with QEA vs 9.2833 s PSO and 7.6833 s BFO; G3: 3.8651 s QEA vs 12.6 s PSO and 8.25 s BFO) for the 100 ms fault scenario.
[supported] QEA-derived optimized PSS and SVC controller parameter sets are presented for both test systems and were used in the comparative simulations.

[supported] In the New England 39-bus case, QEA-based coordinated design reduced undershoot and settling time of several generators versus both an uncoordinated PSS+SVC design and the uncontrolled case.

[speculative] The paper claims QEA overcomes common drawbacks of other evolutionary algorithms (e.g., sensitivity to control-parameter tuning, tendency to get trapped in local optima) — this is argued but only supported by the presented comparative simulations, not by a broader theoretical proof.

[speculative] The authors suggest the coordinated tuning of PSS and SVC via QEA yields improved robustness across operating conditions; while supported in the presented scenarios, general robustness across many operating points is not extensively demonstrated.
results_summary: This empirical study applied a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm (QEA) to the simultaneous tuning of PSS and SVC parameters in two multi-machine power system benchmarks (Kundur 4-machine and New England 39-bus). Time-domain fault simulations (100 ms and 200 ms three-phase faults and 5% voltage reference changes) show that the QEA-tuned coordinated controllers yield faster damping, smaller undershoots, and lower ITAE than comparable designs obtained by PSO and BFO. The paper reports specific reductions in settling time for individual generators and provides the optimized controller parameter sets used in the simulations. The work demonstrates that QEA (as a classical, quantum-inspired heuristic) can be effective for this control-parameter optimization task in the presented cases.
performance_claims: Settling times for 100 ms fault (Kundur 4-machine): G1: QEA 6.1128 s, PSO 9.2833 s, BFO 7.6833 s; G2: QEA 6.9833 s, PSO 7.8667 s, BFO 6.7167 s; G3: QEA 3.8651 s, PSO 12.6 s, BFO 8.25 s; G4: QEA 6.55 s, PSO 10.6795 s, BFO 9.35 s.
Settling times for 200 ms fault (Kundur 4-machine): G1: QEA 6.33 s, PSO 8.6711 s, BFO 8.1 s; G3: QEA 6.3833 s, PSO 10.1579 s, BFO 8.5833 s.
Optimized SVC PI gains (Kundur 4-machine, per table): Kp = 1.4531, Ki = 433.4531 (as reported for the QEA result in Table 5).

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper uses a 'quantum-inspired' evolutionary algorithm (QEA) that implements quantum computing concepts (qubits, rotation gates) as a heuristic on classical computers. The work demonstrates empirical performance benefits of this heuristic versus classical metaheuristics (PSO, BFO) in control tuning tasks for the tested power-system cases, but it does not claim or demonstrate any quantum-computational advantage on quantum hardware. Therefore claims of quantum computational advantage are not applicable.
limitations: Modeling simplifications imposed for computational tractability: for the New England 39-bus case the authors set T2 and T4 = 0.1 and T1 = T3 (explicit modeling constraint to reduce computation).
Fixed SVC siting: the SVC location is pre‑determined at bus 27 based on prior work rather than optimized within the study.
Pre-assumed PSS allocation heuristic: when population generation pattern is not assigned, PSSs are pre‑allocated to generators 5, 7 and 9 as a pre‑assumption (limits search freedom).

Limited scenario set: simulations use a small set of disturbance scenarios (primarily 100 ms and 200 ms three‑phase faults at particular buses and a few voltage step changes), so results are demonstrated on a restricted set of contingencies.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — A quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm (QEA) encoding solutions as qubit vectors and updated via rotation gates achieves lower ITAE and faster settling times than PSO and BFO on Kundur 4-machine and New England 39-bus benchmark tests.

#idea:quantum-advantage — QEA produces concrete optimized controller parameter sets (PSS and SVC PI gains/time-constants) with reported numerical improvements (example ITAE: QEA 0.0138 vs BFO 0.0162 vs PSO 0.0251).

#limitation:simulation-only — All evaluations are classical time-domain simulations using the PSAT toolbox (no quantum hardware or quantum runtime was used), so 'quantum-inspired' refers to algorithmic representation rather than actual quantum computation.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Some QEA hyperparameters (population size, number of generations/termination criteria, random seeds) are not reported, limiting reproducibility of the numerical results.
contradictions: The paper frames improvements as coming from a "quantum" algorithm but uses a quantum-inspired, purely classical evolutionary method; thus claims of quantum advantage are limited to algorithmic inspiration rather than evidence of benefit from quantum hardware.

Although QEA outperforms PSO/BFO on two benchmark systems, the paper omits key hyperparameters (population size, number of generations, termination criteria) and does not assess larger-scale systems, contradicting any implicit claim that the approach is proven to scale to real-world, larger power-system problems.
